links.outcome: Readability grade level of GPT-4 and ophthalmologist responses to patient surgery questions across six metrics
links.effect: GPT-4 responses had higher grade levels than ophthalmologists on all metrics (e.g., FK-GL 13.19 vs 10.71; SMOG 12.18 vs 10.07); both sources required a 12th-grade education.
links.quote: Across all metrics (FK-RE; FK-GL; GFS; SI; CLI; and ARI), GPT-4 responses were at a higher grade level (34.39 [8.51]; 13.19 [2.63]; 16.37 [2.04]; 12.18 [1.43]; 15.72 [1.40]; 12.99 [1.86]) than ophthalmologists' responses (50.61 [15.53]; 10.71 [2.99]; 14.13 [3.55]; 10.07 [2.46]; 12.64 [2.93]; 10.40 [3.61]), with both sources necessitating a 12th-grade education for comprehension.

links.outcome: Reading level of AI and clinician patient materials versus NIH 6th-7th grade recommendation
links.effect: Both GPT-4 and ophthalmologist answers exceeded the NIH 6th- to 7th-grade recommendation, with GPT-4 showing a greater gap; GPT-4 used 24.42% complex words vs 17.76%.
links.quote: Both GPT-4- and ophthalmologist-written answers exceeded this recommendation, with GPT-4 showing a greater gap.

screen.reason: Empirical comparison of the readability of GPT-4 vs. ophthalmologist responses to patient queries using standard readability formulas; does not test a specific safeguard or deployment intervention.
